claims.text: Increasing Al content in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys increases atomic-size mismatch.
Greater atomic-size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
A critical threshold of local lattice distortion exists.
Above the critical distortion threshold, the free-energy balance changes in favor of a dual FCC+BCC microstructure.
A dual FCC+BCC microstructure can simultaneously support high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The baseline is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with standard Al content.
Al content will be varied while the concentrations of all other elements are kept constant.
Annealing at 1100 °C for 24 hours followed by controlled cooling will equilibrate the phases.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used as a measure of local lattice distortion.
High-resolution TEM and synchrotron strain mapping can resolve the proposed nanoscale strain fields.
Increasing Al should produce measurable diffraction-peak broadening and larger local strain fields relative to the baseline.
Elevated local lattice distortion should correlate with a shift in phase fractions toward a stabilized dual-phase mixture.
The baseline alloy has a homogeneous phase structure and lower lattice distortion.
Chemical composition and processing method strongly influence the properties and phase constitution of complex concentrated alloys.
BCC structures generally provide higher hardness but lower fracture toughness, while FCC structures provide lower hardness but higher toughness.
FCC structure and deformation twinning can contribute to high cryogenic strength and ductility in a related CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
The hypothesis is restricted to compositions and processing conditions that produce a detectable change in lattice distortion.
Absence of a statistically significant distortion–phase-fraction correlation, including failure to form the proposed dual phase above the presumed threshold, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention says Al content is varied while all other elemental concentrations remain constant, which is not possible for normalized atomic percentages without specifying a balancing element or dilution convention. The uncertainty field nevertheless refers to difficulty isolating Al from other compositional variables.

The hypothesis and falsification rule rely on exceeding a critical distortion threshold, but the threshold is neither defined nor quantified and is explicitly described as uncertain, making the threshold-based part of the falsification rule operationally ambiguous.
